author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Tide Between Us
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
Vel was sitting at our kitchen table when I came home.

I recognized the small wooden fish beside her cup. It was the one she'd returned after Maui refused to shame Tomas for leaving Lanternweald. I hadn't seen her since.

Maui stood at the stove looking uncomfortable.

"Jasper," he said, "Vel needs a place to stay until the north road clears."

I looked from him to her.

"Does she?"

Vel lifted her chin. "My cart axle broke. The shelter is full."

"The shelter isn't full," I said, because I'd helped with the count that afternoon. "There are rooms available on the upper level."

Maui shot me a warning glance.

Vel looked wounded.

I put down my bag.

"Can we talk outside?" I asked Maui.

He followed me to the porch. The sea wind was strong enough to make the lantern shiver on its hook.

"You brought someone into our home without asking," I said.

"She needed help."

"Yes. She deserves help. That's not the same as deciding she can sleep here."

"She's had a hard day."

"So have I."

He looked at me.

"You're being harsh."

I felt something hot and unpleasant rise behind my ribs.

"And you're being generous with space that isn't only yours."

His face changed. We stood very still.

Then the door opened and Vel stepped onto the porch.

"I can hear you," she said.

I closed my eyes.

"Vel, I'm sorry. You shouldn't have had to listen to us argue over your head."

She looked from me to Maui.

"I thought he said I could stay."

"He did," Maui answered quietly. "Without checking with Jasper first. That's my mistake."

Vel's mouth tightened.

"Then I'll go."

"Not into the rain," I said. "There's a room at the hall. I can walk you there and help with the cart arrangements tomorrow, if you'd like."

She stared at me.

"I don't want charity."

"Then we can talk about the actual cost of the room. The hall has a posted rate for people who can pay, and emergency funds for people who can't. You decide what you want to share."

Vel looked away.

After a moment she nodded.

Maui fetched her bag. He offered to escort her, but she asked me instead. The choice seemed to hurt him; he didn't argue.

We walked to the hall along the safe ridge. Vel spoke only once.

"I thought if I came back, he'd forgive me for being angry."

"He might," I said. "But you don't have to stay in his house to talk to him."

She looked at me sharply.

"I didn't want to make trouble."

"I believe you."

We checked the room. It was clean, dry, and had a working lamp. A volunteer explained how the door locked from the inside. Vel accepted the key and asked whether Mara would be selling bread in the morning.

"She will."

"Good."

When I returned home, Maui was washing the cups. He'd scrubbed the table, too, as though the wood itself had taken part in the argument.

"She's safe?" he asked.

"Yes."

He nodded.

I took off my coat.

"I don't want to fight," I said.

"Neither do I."

"Then we have to talk about what happened."

He set down the cloth.

"I wanted to prove I could still help her. After Tomas left, she stopped believing in me. I thought if I gave her a place to stay, she might understand."

"That's not your house to give alone."

"I know."

I sat across from him.

"Your kindness became an unasked favor from me. And when I objected, you made me sound cruel."

He looked stricken.

"You're right."

I held up a hand. "I wasn't fair either. I corrected Vel in front of you both instead of asking what she needed. I treated her like a problem before I'd even listened."

Maui exhaled.

"We were trying to be good people."

"We were trying to look like good people," I said. "At least a little."

He gave a rueful laugh.

That was the beginning of the repair, not the end.

We talked about shared space. We agreed that either of us could offer immediate help in a true emergency, but an overnight guest required discussion when both of us were available. If someone needed shelter and our answer was no, we would help them find an alternative rather than leave them without options.

Maui wrote it beneath our calendar agreement, in the same enormous handwriting.

Then he stared at the page.

"Do you still want to live with me?"

I looked at the sink full of cups and the crooked fish drawing beside the stove.

"Yes," I said. "But wanting doesn't remove the work."

He came around the table, slowly enough for me to choose whether to meet him.

"Can I hold you?"

I stood.

He wrapped his arms around me. His breath shook once against my hair.

"I'm sorry," he whispered.

"So am I."

I lifted my face. His kiss was gentle, then warmer when I drew him closer. There were no fireworks, no perfect words, and no audience. Later we closed the door and left the rest of the night between us.

In the morning, Maui went to the hall.

He asked Vel whether she wanted to talk. She told him not yet.

He accepted it.

He returned with bread from Mara, a message that Vel's cart would be repaired after the morning inspection, and the uncomfortable realization that apology didn't entitle him to immediate forgiveness.

We ate breakfast together.

The tide was coming in.

For once, neither of us mistook that movement for a reason to hurry.
